These successes are largely attributed to the adoption of large-scale convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on massive datasets. An increasing number of modern high-performance computing facilities are dedicating significant resources to training even larger ANNs. This computing power has enabled the training of ultra-scale networks containing trillions of parameters. Despite the success of these large models, their computational and memory demands often exceed available resources, limiting the ability to train state-of-the-scale networks within reasonable timeframes.

To address these constraints, we introduce a straightforward and effective method for speedup and memory efficiency in training deep neural networks. Our approach achieves more than a threefold acceleration in wall-clock time, doubles GPU memory capacity, leverages mixed-precision training, and incorporates robust regularizers such as dropout and weight decay. Unlike many existing solutions, our method requires no modifications to standard training loops and avoids additional code complexities.

We validate our technique across various large-scale CNN architectures, including ResNet, ResNeXt, EfficientNet, and Vision Transformers. These models were trained on ImageNet and other benchmarks, with evaluations of our proposed method, comparisons against current state-of-the-art techniques, and analyses of training dynamics. Our findings offer significant implications and potential applications, especially considering the recent release of new and even more powerful supercomputers. We introduce a theoretical model of play based on Poisson processes to examine how strategic decisions impact the probability of scoring and, consequently, game outcomes. The model features teams selecting locations to create shots and players assessing whether those locations yield goals. These choices are evaluated against opposing team defenses and grounded in spatial statistics, game theory, and optimization. Simulations reveal a complex, non-trivial asymmetry in the noise-driven transition from competing to polarized states. By assigning different Hurst exponents to the two parties, we effectively test various scenarios of noise strength asymmetry. Furthermore, we analyze the competition under the same noise intensity, which aligns with standard noisy voter models, using these findings to contextualize our results on opinion polarization under competing asymmetries. Our primary contribution is the identification of three distinct regimes under competing noise asymmetry: (R1) the intensity of the louder party dictates the scaling of average polarization; (R2) the dominant factor is the intensity of the quieter party, leading to full polarization regardless of its magnitude; and (R3) the combined intensities of both parties govern the scaling, a state that may represent self-censorship or fear-induced total polarization. These findings are validated across diverse parameter ranges and system sizes, with implications for analyzing polarization under real-world noise conditions. The reported R2 and R3 regimes offer novel insights, contrasting with existing literature that often assumes symmetric noise. Our study confirms that 1D voter models with noisy boundaries exhibit similar behaviors to those with noisy bulk dynamics. We also provide an analytical derivation of the prefixing phenomenon observed in R3. Finally, we extend the discussion to asymmetric noisy voter models where both the noise source and boundary conditions are asymmetric. Under R2 and R3, the average polarization follows a square-root scaling law, but the prefactors differ. We offer an analytical explanation for this discrepancy and validate it numerically. Under R1, the prefactors are identical. Additionally, we address the misconception that the same Hurst exponent in a competing noisy voter model implies symmetric noise intensity.

the need to further automate and remotely manage experiments has become evident. This project details the technical creation of a two-dimensional (2D) Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) measurement utilizing a single-point LDV system via an automated, remote-controlled workflow. The goal of this report is to facilitate the rapid deployment of setups for comparable applications. Additionally, the described configuration is modular and has been employed to evaluate the modal response of samples excited by both acoustic and mechanical forces. While this single-point LDV method entails a slightly lower data acquisition rate compared to scanning techniques and superior multi-point systems, its significant benefit lies in requiring fewer optical components, making it more robust and easier to maintain, especially in remote environments. Furthermore, the emphasis in this report lies on the quantitative analysis achieved through advanced post-processing techniques applied to the point-clouds gathered from single-point LDV recordings. These methods successfully overcame limitations in spatial resolution and excitation targeting, accurately localizing the position and frequency of modes excited by a sonicator (approx. 20-200 Hz) and a mechanical actuator (approx. 500 Hz - 3.5 kHz). However, this post-processing approach is universally applicable to any point-cloud obtained from an LDV, enabling the investigation of lower-frequency modes generated by alternative excitation sources, such as a laser-induced breakdown remote sensor (LIBS). Furthermore, the enhanced remote controllability of this setup facilitates the expansion of the study to other phenomena, including those related to material science, fluid dynamics, or acoustics. The increased automation of the workflow not only reduces the time required to conduct experiments but also minimizes the necessity for highly skilled operators, rendering it exceptionally well-suited for the current era of increased remote experimentation. This is particularly advantageous for accelerating post-pandemic scientific endeavors involving live virus interaction or high-risk material testing, where non-contact measurement is crucial and rapid data acquisition is essential. Ultimately, this approach offers a more cost-effective and resilient alternative to commercial solutions, which often rely on complex optics and are prohibitively expensive. Although the single-point LDV post-processing method was optimized for specific frequency ranges, it is not limited to these; with minor adjustments to the post-processing workflow, the technique can be adapted to identify modes across a broader spectrum, limited only by the sampling rate, which can be enhanced through more affordable and high-performance camera upgrades.

This approach significantly surpasses traditional vectorization methods, such as Glaser et al. (2019), that average word representations, particularly for lexically polysemous items. Second, we present a qualitative analysis of specific instances selected from the model's outputs, demonstrating how these outputs reflect genuine, non-spurious diachronic semantic changes. Our findings indicate that, when properly configured, contextualized embedding methods can identify authentic, gradual shifts in word meanings over time without being unduly influenced by extraneous factors like morphological variations, positional biases, or data noise. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for computational research into the evolution of word meanings and the acquisition of semantics and polysemy in neural language models. Our code and datasets are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedshoukry/Time2Meaning.

This study examines the spin of a specific class of type-1 AGN featuring broad H$\beta$ emission lines, utilizing high-resolution optical spectra from the SDSS and the 10.4-meter Keck II telescope. By applying a semi-analytical approach to six-color imaging from public surveys, we identify the mass of the central black hole ($M_{\rm BH}$) through the full profile of the H$\beta$ emission line, a method that yields masses typically ranging from $10^7$ to $10^9~M_{\odot}$ for these objects. We also assess the feasibility of determining $M_{\rm BH}$ from the full MgII emission line profile. The resulting masses show good agreement with those derived from other methods, such as the $V-r$ velocity dispersion ($\sigma$), although the $\sigma$-mass relation exhibits significant scatter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the FWHM of the H$\beta$ line can be expressed as a power law of $\sigma$, with a slope of $0.60\pm0.03$ that aligns well with findings from other studies. The broad-line region (BLR) masses inferred from the H$\beta$ and MgII profiles fall within the range expected from Keplerian dynamics at their observed radii. However, the BLR masses derived from the H$\beta$ profile are generally higher than previous estimates based on the full line profile, likely due to the inclusion of a low-velocity component corresponding to stellar atmospheres. These BLR masses are consistent with the $V-r$ velocity dispersion when the BLR radius ($R_{\rm BLR}$) is calculated using the general relativistic light bending relation $R_{\rm BLR}\approx 2.6~R_{\rm S} (a_{\rm BH}/0.99)^{1.5}$, where $R_{\rm S}=2GM_{\rm BH}/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius and $a_{\rm BH}=c^2L/(GM_{\rm BH}\dot{M}})$ is the black hole's specific angular momentum. movement of nuclei between the apical and basal surfaces of the neuroepithelium, known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid, and three-dimensional live imaging of zebrafish retinas to examine IKNM during rapid retinal neurogenesis in 1- and 2-day-old larvae. During these early stages, migration slows considerably compared to earlier retinal genesis, coinciding with the onset of asymmetric cell division and the initiation of neuronal migration. We demonstrate that nuclear movement during these asymmetric divisions retains core principles of IKNM: it adheres to a "railroad track" mechanism mediated by the same cytoskeletal and motor proteins, exhibits a periodic, "tug-of-war" motion characterized by competing apical and basal forces, and involves nuclei ceasing migration precisely at their destination to complete division. Furthermore, these asymmetric divisions are spatially organized, with more mature daughter cells positioned further from the apical surface. By integrating imaging with quantitative analysis and genetic manipulations, we further reveal that the duration of IKNM in 1-day-old larvae is regulated by the accumulation of cell cycle inhibitors, such as GATA-3 and p27, in the basal compartment. Collectively, these findings indicate that while the fundamental mechanisms of IKNM remain consistent across retinogenesis in zebrafish, the process is dynamically regulated to coordinate cell fate decisions, maturation, and cell cycle progression as development proceeds. These genetic and physical constraints on IKNM likely serve as a unifying framework for understanding how diverse cell type maturation and fate decisions occur during early retinal neurogenesis in zebrafish and potentially across vertebrates. Live imaging techniques and analytical methods employed for this work are accessible online, enabling the characterization of nuclear behaviors in other interkinetically migrating populations throughout zebrafish retinal development. Live videos are available at https://video.yale.edu/showcase/iknm-and-asymmetric-cell-division-zebrafish-retina and analysis scripts can be found at https://github.com/yalebiophysics/AsymmetricCellDivisionAnalysis.

In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack the incoherence properties found in random patterns, which can result in poor reconstruction quality. This paper introduces a new class of code patterns designed to facilitate the recovery of constituent images in video compressed sensing and demosaicing tasks. These codes integrate the advantages of both positive and random patterns while maintaining compatibility with existing systems. By leveraging the group-by-4 structure of current Bayer demosaicing cameras, the proposed Bayer Coded Sensing (BCS) pattern enhances the recoverability of constituent images through a low-rank prior. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach yields superior video quality, achieving a PSNR improvement of approximately 1.5 dB over existing Bayer coded sensing methods, while also reducing the sampling rate by half compared to random patterns. The BCS pattern is now publicly available to accelerate future research in video compressed sensing and demosaicing.

Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Despite this limitation, we derive the precise dimension-dependent scaling exponents for these ranges. These findings are derived using a renormalization group approach grounded in stochastic hydrodynamics, which accurately balances the driving mechanisms in two dimensions against hydrodynamic advection and quenched disorder. Finally, we provide an overview of open questions regarding the dimensional scaling exponents in dimensions greater than 5.

Active matter consists of systems comprising many interacting self-propelled particles that have become a significant area of research across experimental and theoretical domains. This interest is particularly driven by the lack of equilibrium in these systems, resulting in rich, yet under-explored, nonequilibrium phenomena. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop a comprehensive understanding of active systems through a robust theoretical lens. This manuscript begins by introducing the fundamentals of a 1D 1C (line) hydrodynamic model for 1D, 2D, and higher-dimensional systems. Subsequently, it examines the role of quenched randomness in driving line dancing within 2D and 3D spaces, followed by an analysis of fractional self-mobility across dimensions. The document concludes with suggestions for future research directions. This work represents a revised and expanded iteration of arXiv:2006.09528.

In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in the nonequilibrium dynamics of one-dimensional (1D) active matter, fueled by significant theoretical and experimental breakthroughs. This research area is often referred to as line-decimals, a term coined to describe the intricate behaviors observed in 1D systems. This work presents a revised and expanded version of arXiv:2006.095D. It starts by outlining the motivations for studying hydrodynamic models of Q-2D and Q-3D active systems, which are then used to investigate line dancing dynamics. The paper also explores the effects of fractional self-mobility in various dimensions and offers suggestions for future research directions. This work serves as an extended and updated iteration of arXiv:2006.09528.

Keywords: active matter; hydrodynamics; nonequilibrium

Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent identity theft. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the retrieval of specific data within text. Conversely, NLP enables computers to understand, process, and generate human language. This study focuses on extracting data from KKU (Kartu Keluarga Indonesia) cards using Python. The extraction methodology involves several stages: first, OpenCV is used to capture the ID card image, followed by converting it to grayscale and applying Gaussian blurring to reduce noise. Second, OCR is employed to locate lines containing the name and birthdate. Third, NLP helps determine the coordinates of the photo and name sections. Fourth, contour finding isolates the ID card's boundaries, followed by perspective warping to correct skew and produce a rectangular image. Finally, the extracted photo and name are saved. For the birthdate, contours are located similarly to the name, the image is cut into segments, and OCR is reapplied to each segment to find the accurate coordinates. WORPress OCR then processes the resulting text to extract the birthdate. Evaluation results on 50 ID cards show a precision of 0.98, a recall of 0.96, and an F-score of 0.97 for the name, with an evaluation score of 0.96 for the photo. The completed code is available at https://github.com/putriyusafah/OCR-NLP-untuk-Extract-Data-dari-KKU. (English) (OCR) (NLP) (KKU) (ID Card) (F-Score)

group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, the symmetry groups of any surface with a boundary—regarded as a group under the Roelcke topology—fail to be precompact. This result extends to surfaces without a boundary when considered as groups under the right uniformity. These findings reinforce the well-established notion that the zero-extension of the Roelcke topology on $Homeo(M)$ is not right uniformly continuous, as shown by S. Monsky. Our conclusions also hold for the alternative extension, which is characterized by the inequality $d(\sigma\tau, id) \leq C(d(\sigma, id) + d(\tau, id))$ for all $\sigma, \tau$. We further determine the specific constants associated with every such locally Roelcke precompact subgroup. These results have significant implications for distinguishing between various topologies on transformation groups, including their application to the non-Archimedean topology on homeomorphisms recently introduced by Y. Shklyarov. Additionally, our work clarifies the relationship between the right and left uniformities on Roelcke topologies, generalizing the triangle inequality to $\sup_{\sigma} d_L(\sigma, id) \leq 2 \sup_{\tau} d_R(\tau, id)$ over a locally Roelcke precompact set. This characterization reveals that a subgroup of $Homeo(M)$ with the Roelcke topology is precisely those where the left uniformity is bounded by the right uniformity up to a factor of 2. These observations remain valid when replacing "Roelcke" with "right" or "left" uniformity. As a byproduct, we provide a boundedness criterion for the left uniformity on a subgroup of $Homeo(M)$ endowed with the right uniformity, thereby offering a novel perspective on the Zariski density of a subgroup within the simple group of germs at the origin for a surface. Our primary contribution lies in quantifying the constants involved. These results extend to the setting of surfaces with conical singularities.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this result extends to computability via the work of \cite{DBLP:conf:sss:Choffrut10}. Additionally, we establish that continuous regular functions are precisely the piecewise affine functions composed with the booleanization map, which allows us to decide computability for such functions and highlights the existence of infinitely many non-computable continuous regular functions. To achieve these findings, we develop results on the composition and image of functions that are piecewise affine with respect to the Cantor topology. Along the way, we also decide approximability for a broader class of functions encompassing rational functions and prove that continuous functions are exactly those that are both approximable and co-approximable. These decisions are made without relying on the Myhill-Nerode theorem; instead, we employ a characterization of equivalence relations with finitely many equivalence classes based on the existence of a finite quotient topological space. Along the way, we generalize previous findings on the composition and image of piecewise affine functions to apply to continuous regular functions. The proofs of our main contributions are available in a machine-checkable format on our website: \url{https://www.haibozhou.com/research/week5a/}.

A key benefit of this approach is its ability to guarantee accurate short-term predictions. However, because exact predictions are eventually inevitable, guaranteeing these accurate predictions beyond the initial period remains a challenge. This paper examines methods to ensure accurate short-term predictions in recurrent reservoir computers over extended durations. We evaluate these methods across multiple dynamical system types, including a time series representing solar wind plasma characteristics at Earth and various chaotic Lorentz reservoir computing models. Our findings indicate that these guarantee strategies are broadly effective, resulting in surrogate models that are both highly accurate and robust. Furthermore, we demonstrate that enforcing these guarantees allows for surrogate models with larger reservoir dimensions that are harder to train. The findings also suggest that this approach is particularly advantageous for dynamical systems exhibiting rare, high-impact events. By accurately predicting these events, the strategy enhances the capability to predict anomalies in real-time. Consequently, guaranteeing accurate short-term predictions in reservoir computing represents a potent strategy for building high-fidelity surrogate models of complex dynamical systems, thereby expanding the practical applications of reservoir computers.

Operating on a discretized grid of the state space, our method contrasts with established Eulerian techniques by utilizing a Lagrangian framework. Specifically, we apply a backward-in-time sweep to establish state constraints, followed by solving for worst-case disturbance constraints along state trajectories. As the resulting state and disturbance are constrained respectively by these two spaces, we employ an integration method based on state-phase flow to address the problem within a Lagrangian setting. We implement this approach both globally for bounded state constraints and locally, offering an approximate solution for sayable states within an unknown horizon. Validation against the traditional Eulerian method demonstrates that the proposed algorithm achieves a significant reduction in the number of unconstrained states, a finding with direct implications for state estimation. Furthermore, we offer a novel perspective on state estimation by addressing it as a two-player game between the system and noise, governed by the HJI equation, and show how the Lagrangian solution corresponds to the filter density. The global solution addresses constrained states (represented as the product of state and disturbance magnitudes), while the local solution addresses constrained state neighborhoods (defined as a matrix). Crucially, the global solution serves as the foundation for a recursive filter, as the local solution can be derived from it. Finally, we confirm that the Lagrangian method is inherently adaptive to the current state. Derived from first principles, this work establishes a new benchmark for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HBJ) and variational Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) equations within the "curse of dimensionality" framework. The global solution is achieved via a sweep algorithm without the need for specified time or state horizons, relying solely on constraints defined by hyper-ellipsoids. In contrast, the local solution leverages an approximate solution within a bounded domain, employing a max-pooling mechanism to handle the unknown horizon for the disturbance. Consequently, the computational complexity of the global solution is $O(n)$, and the local solution maintains comparable efficiency, representing a substantial improvement over the traditional Eulerian $O(n^2)$ complexity. This study examines these mechanisms using a large-scale electrophysiological dataset from macaque V4. We introduced a novel approach to analyze temporal representational geometry by identifying the best-fitting statistical manifold that encodes stimuli based on their animacy. Our analysis reveals that Animacy-Manifolds exist in V4, successfully representing both animal and non-animal stimuli with an accuracy approximately 50% higher than random chance. Furthermore, we observed that the intrinsic dimensionality of these manifolds scales positively with the number of non-animal stimuli. When compared to alternative representational models, the Animacy-Manifold most accurately captures neural data from living animals, suggesting it reflects representations driven by biological motion and form. Comparisons across monkeys with varying ages of animation experience indicate that the representational structure of Animacy-Manifolds in V4 is experience-dependent. These results suggest that processes relevant to animacy—specifically biological motion and form—are encoded in V4, and this experience-dependent organization arises from biologically significant stimuli. These electrophysiological findings align with representational models derived from fMRI data in V4/VTC of humans. We propose that the ambiguous nature of animacy results in less ambiguous, experience-dependent neural code distributions, which manifest as low-dimensional statistical manifolds in VTC of macaques.

This letter demonstrates that during such events, the effective $R_0$ value becomes extremely high, reaching hundreds or even exceeding a thousand. These findings were derived from time-series data of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Los Angeles County, New York City, and Wuhan, covering periods that include both intense super-spreader events and subsequent gradual outbreak expansions. The analysis indicates that $R_0$ values of 10 or lower, often assumed as typical, are actually observed only during gradual, non super-spreader outbreak phases. Furthermore, the study validates the well-mixed assumption for subsequent outbreak expansions, supporting the use of the SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered) model with an effective $R_0$ of approximately 3 for these events. We explicitly identify the timestamps when outbreaks transition into super-spreader events and determine their magnitude. By illustrating how inferring the number of primary cases from these timestamps relies on estimates of $R_0$, infectious period, and reporting fractions, we offer a distinct approach to estimating primary case numbers that does not depend on specific reporting fractions. Finally, comparing outbreaks before and after stringent interventions in Los Angeles and New York reveals that while $R_0$ dropped dramatically—from around 5.8 to 1.9—other factors also significantly influenced the epidemic curve. These insights are directly applicable to evaluating super-spreader occurrences in future outbreaks.

While modern spectrographs typically achieve a radial velocity precision better than 1 m/s, this level of accuracy necessitates a full characterization of all potential biases. Although a 1 m/s precision seems sufficient for most exoplanet research, it is insufficient for detecting ultra-low-mass planets orbiting close to their host stars or for high-significance tests of the mass and obliquity of super-Earths and Neptune-mass planets. To date, no comprehensive study has quantified the combined biases from unmodeled instrumental factors in ESPRESSO radial velocities. By analyzing 1000 spectra of the star HD 217107, we determined that the true radial velocities of HD 217107's two planets are obscured by ESPRESSO biases ranging from several to over 10 cm/s. Specifically, we found a median bias of 2.1 m/s in the out-of-pixel y-direction and identified an additional, previously unreported, 1 cm/s bias associated with the order-sorting filter position. We observed no significant biases related to the CCD tilt angle, the number of orders per exposure, or the exposure order (1st or 2nd). These identified biases are now incorporated into the analysis of ESPRESSO radial velocities for known exoplanets and are available to the broader community at the provided repository. Furthermore, applying these corrections to the smallest obliquity measurement to date for an oblique Neptune—$\Psi_{HD~217107C} = 81^{+14}_{-13} degrees$—results in a reduced obliquity of $\Psi = 70.5^{+10.5}_{-10.0} degrees$ at 68.3% confidence, an decrease greater than 3 sigma when accounting for measurement errors. While this transformation introduces a Jacobian determinant into the Boltzmann weight—manageable for small systems—we investigate whether the determinant can be factored into a mean-field term and a remainder that can be treated via perturbation theory. This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. We introduce ReCross, a retrieval-augmentation approach that utilizes a few unlabeled examples as queries to fetch a targeted subset of upstream data, thereby updating the model to improve its generalization performance. ReCross represents a simple yet potent retrieval strategy that integrates efficient dense retrieval with effective pairwise reranking. Empirical results and analysis demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses both non-retrieval approaches and other baseline techniques. Specifically, after adaptive pretraining augmented with unlabeled data, our approach successfully combines the strengths of BERT and T0, exceeding state-of-the-art results and surpassing the retrieval-based few-shot baseline by an average of 3.09 (with a maximum improvement of 5.6) ILP points on the zero-shot generalization test of the T0 benchmark. Furthermore, our approach yields superior results on the original few-shot tests of T0 and in additional cross-domain generalization scenarios. Even a simplified version of our method proves effective when applied to various domains and tasks. We have made our code and model publicly available here.

This issue is particularly acute in large-scale settings where private models are trained on extensive datasets. This paper focuses on a key hyperparameter in DPSGD: the noise scale added to gradients. We propose an efficient adaptive method for adjusting this parameter that requires minimal computation, making it especially beneficial for large-scale data. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, confirming both its efficiency and its ability to optimize privacy-accuracy trade-offs. While a linear model effectively captures long-term trends, a linear fit residual plot reveals distinct short-term patterns, including a multi-year cycle ranging from 3.5 to 4.8 years, an annual cycle, and a semi-annual cycle, all of which can be explained by known drivers. To further investigate these patterns, we apply an Empirical Wavelet Transform (EWT) to decompose the data into various time-scale components. This decomposition allows for separate analysis of trends across decades, as well as medium and short-term cycles like those observed since the 1960s. By integrating EWT results with findings from the linear model, we achieve a more comprehensive understanding of CO$_2$ changes at Mauna Loa. Specifically, we quantify the amplitude and phase of cycles operating on different time scales, such as the dominant multi-year cycle (approximately 4.1 years since the 1960s) and the annual cycle, which have average amplitudes of roughly 1.30 ppm and 0.16 ppm, respectively, over recent decades. These findings highlight that atmospheric CO$_2$ variations at Mauna Loa consist of multiple superimposed cycles on top of a consistent upward linear trend. Consequently, relying solely on a linear model to describe long-term trends may lead to misinterpretations when analyzing shorter periods of CO$_2$ variations. The multiple time-scale cycles detected through EWT at Mauna Loa can be accounted for by established factors, including land use changes, El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and the Northern Hemisphere's seasonal cycle. Additionally, the W5E5 climate model successfully reproduces the primary multi-year cycle and the annual cycle at Mauna Loa, supporting the plausibility of these variations. Ultimately, this linear model combined with EWT provides a robust framework for dissecting atmospheric CO$_2$ changes at Mauna Loa, facilitating more accurate monitoring and analysis of these critical fluctuations.

In this work, we demonstrate that this intriguing result stems from the specific parametrization $1+(1+z)$ employed for the dark energy equation of state $w$. Furthermore, we highlight how the 1-term and 2-term Taylor expansions of any observational data point naturally decompose into components scaling as $1/(1+z)^2$ and $1/z$, respectively. This decomposition offers a straightforward explanation for why fitting methods emphasizing recent epochs yield increasingly smaller estimates for $w$. Most importantly, we show that existing data currently available offer no evidence for an equation of state $w$ that varies slowly with redshift in the high-$z$ regime. Consequently, the current consensus on a constant equation of state $w \simeq -1$ likely results from a parametrization bias, suggesting that $w$ could potentially be positive in the very high-$z$ range. This conclusion starkly contrasts with the established view of an accelerating universe at lower redshifts. If $w$ were indeed positive at high $z$, the universe would have experienced recollapsing eras, causing it to expand and contract like a closed or open system. By employing a robust probabilistic approach that incorporates observational data, theoretical constraints, and cosmological principles, we determine the expansion history $a(t)$ solely based on the fact that the universe is expanding now ($\dot{a}_0 > 0$). Our results indicate a probability $P(w<0)=0.68^{+0.19}_{-0.16}$ for the dark energy equation of state being negative, and $P(w>0.6)=0.22$ for it to exceed $0.6$. These findings align with a probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics applied to a closed universe, which posits $w>1$ (a positive Casimir effect). Ultimately, the expansion history of our universe could be explained by a fluctuating vacuum energy density, causing the universe to expand and collapse cyclically over eons.

Introduction

Creating a thorough representation of fundamental, commonsense knowledge across numerous domains is vital for the development of Artificial Intelligence. This is particularly relevant for " Everyday Commonsense," which supports basic human activities. Although prior research has explored commonsense in areas like dialogue understanding and social media analysis, existing datasets lack depth and are often limited to specific contexts. In this paper, we present the ATOMIC atlas of everyday commonsense, a comprehensive collection of general knowledge subgraphs. We start by examining prior work on structured and unstructured commonsense, followed by an overview of the ATOMIC project. Next, we describe our methodology for curating the atlas and building knowledge subgraphs, and we assess the quality of our general knowledge subgraphs using external evaluations. Finally, we highlight the diverse domains covered by the ATOMIC atlas.

Prior Research on Commonsense

Structured Commonsense

Recent initiatives have sought to systematically organize and represent commonsense knowledge. The Cycle Knowledge Project structures this around three interconnected graphs: things, events, and why. These graphs are interconnected via causal and entailment links, forming a "Cycle Knowledge" subgraph. While this project offers a thorough representation of fundamental concepts, its scope is limited compared to the ATOMIC atlas, which covers a broader range of domains.

### I. Introduction

The field of automatic speech recognition (ASR) is rapidly evolving, with recent breakthroughs driven by end-to-end ASR models. These architectures directly map acoustic features to character- or phoneme-level outputs, utilizing techniques like attention mechanisms to manage the variable sequence lengths between audio and text. Representative models in this category include Listen-Attend-Spell (LAS) and its derivative Transformer-based LAS (TransLAS), which have achieved state-of-the-art results across various datasets.

A defining characteristic of these models is their capacity to leverage auxiliary supervision, such as phoneme signals, to lower dependency on massive text data. By integrating phoneme-level annotations, LAS and TransLAS have demonstrated improved performance even with sparse phoneme labels. However, acquiring dense phoneme annotations remains a significant hurdle, as most available signals are sparse compared to the model capacity, and existing alignment tools often fail to meet the quality standards needed for large-scale datasets.

In this work, we introduce novel automatic and semi-automatic pipelines to generate dense phoneme annotations, enabling the training of end-to-end ASR models. Our goal is to facilitate the development of high-capacity architectures by providing access to dense phoneme signals through two strategies that overcome current limitations. matrix $H$ defined on an infinite regular tree, where entries are typically independent and centered but exhibit long-range correlations. The matrix $H$ serves as a generalization of the Ginibre matrix, incorporating the local correlations essential for the latter's distinctive behavior. Specifically, we establish that the spectral measure of any node converges to the semi-circle law, implying the Wigner-Semicircle law for the average linear statistics of eigenvalues, a result that is particularly notable given the sparsity of the matrix. However, the convergence of the spectral measure to the semi-circle law does not automatically ensure the validity of the eigenvalue statistics characteristic of typical Wigner matrices. To achieve the latter, the fluctuations of the spectral measure must also align with the universal behaviors observed in standard ensembles. Unfortunately, $H$ does not belong to a typical universality class. We prove that, for any two fixed indices $j$ and $k$, the full collection of normalized squared differences between the $j$-th and $k$-th eigenvalues associated with sites $j$ and $k$ follows the circular law. This finding extends a recent result by Ben Arous, Guionnet, and Maier, which only addressed the two-point squared distances of eigenvalues. Additionally, we indicate the directions in which the spectrum of $H$ diverges from the typical spectral properties of large, sparse matrices. An appendix, authored by Ben Arous, Lyu, and Senat, demonstrates the convergence to the circular law for the three-point squared distances of eigenvalues. The establishment of the circular law for $H$ represents a significant finding, as the matrix's tri-clustering structure places it outside the scope of existing methods used to prove the circular law for other models. Our approach relies on the supersymmetric formalism, adapting key techniques from recent literature on the spectral density of large, sparse, typical Hermitian random matrices to derive a self-consistent equation for the Stieltjes transform of $H$. This equation confirms the circular law while also providing the framework for the stated convergence results and highlighting how $H$'s spectrum differs from that of standard sparse ensembles. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work to matrices with broader self-consistent structures.

This study introduces an advanced modeling framework designed to quantify these processes within classroom settings and assess their impact on infection risk. The model comprises three key components: first, it accurately simulates the emission, spatial distribution, and temporal evolution of aerosols released by individuals; second, it calculates the inhalation rate of these aerosols by vulnerable persons; and third, it integrates human dynamics and susceptibility to determine the overall infection probability. These capabilities were initially validated using a simplified scenario involving an emitting source and a single recipient, with results cross-checked against established infection probability formulas. The resulting risk profiles offer school administrators and health officials quantitative insights into how volunteer ventilation choices interact with classroom-specific factors to either mitigate or exacerbate viral spread. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. In this study, we investigate how the spin-orbit coupling within a monolayer graphene defect embedded in a graphene oxide matrix influences graphene's electronic properties. Our findings indicate that even a minimal local increase in spin-orbit coupling, amounting to only a few meV, can drastically alter the monolayer's low-energy excitations. Specifically, the emergence of Majorana fermions becomes possible when the combined effective spin-orbit coupling from both sides of the monolayer surpasses the charge-induced coupling. Furthermore, we constructed a magnetic Brillouin zone to analyze the interplay between various symmetries and mapped out the full spectrum of excited states. Our results demonstrate that the intricate symmetry breaking patterns arising from the coexistence of magnetic order, lattice symmetry, and spin-orbit coupling enable the generation of highly nontrivial topological phases. These phases can give rise to robust, chiral electronic states confined to the edges or defects of the monolayer. This mechanism offers a viable approach to engineering exotic states of matter, such as the quantum anomalous Hall effect, using graphene defects on oxidized substrates. To achieve this, precise control over the magnitude and asymmetry of the spin-orbit proximity effect is essential, which can be accomplished by manipulating the substrate's dielectric and magnetic properties. This is particularly significant for the development of efficient spin-orbit based electronics. The study includes a comprehensive analysis of symmetry breaking patterns, a derivation of the band structure in the presence of competing effects, and an examination of the consequences on the surface state spectrum. These outcomes are fully consistent with recent experimental observations. We provide a robust theoretical framework based on tight-binding models to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and derive analytical expressions for the involved parameters. Our findings can be directly validated through recent and upcoming experimental techniques, including angle- and photo-induced photoemission spectroscopy, scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and nano-Fourier transform photoconductivity measurements.

**1 Introduction**

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet it has consistently been criticized for lacking interpretability. While this may be acceptable in many applications, it is often unacceptable in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. Additionally, the field has recently encountered scalability issues, where recent performance gains stem largely from larger models and datasets rather than novel architectures or training techniques. These problems are exacerbated by the vulnerability of neural networks to adversarial attacks and other generalization barriers, which have limited the impact of recent advancements. Although researchers have explored various solutions, existing approaches have yet to deliver significant, scalable improvements. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularizer that addresses multiple generalized concerns simultaneously. Specifically, we show that explicitly regularizing a neural network so that it is Lipschitz continuous with respect to its inputs (under a norm of choice) leads to models that are more robust, generalizable, and, in many cases, more interpretable than those using prior regularizers.

., 1995) offers a linguistic framework for analyzing discourse structure, positing that local coherence emerges from how successive utterances reference shared entities. This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why CT yields minimal improvements for modern neural systems utilizing pretrained representations. Finally, we address coreference factors unmodeled by standard CT, such as world knowledge and recency bias. By formulating an enhanced version of CT that incorporates recency, we show it captures coreference information more effectively than the original formulation. Overall, our findings suggest that while coreference and centering are intrinsically linked, modern neural systems implicitly handle these aspects so well that they no longer require the standard CT assumptions. Consequently, researchers developing neural coreference resolvers are not obligated to adhere to Centering Theory. (OpenReview.net)

This concern is especially pertinent to multi-pass Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs), where even modest charge quantities can generate substantial beam-rope currents. This study examines an ERL design intended for atom probe microscopy, demonstrating that, given its specific parameters, beam breakup is likely to limit operational beam current. We further investigate how modifying key ERL parameters—such as the initial accelerating structure length, recirculator radius, number of passes, and bunch length—could mitigate beam breakup concerns while maintaining suitability for atom probe applications. The findings offer guidance for selecting ERL parameters that avoid beam breakup instability for proposed medium-scale ERLs targeting this use case, suggesting a potential reduction in the initial accelerating structure length to as little as 10 cm for the 50 mErl design under examination. Although a complete global optimization of a an proton ERL for atom probe microscopy remains beyond the scope of this paper, our results indicate that an approximately 300 m recirculator could be shortened to around 200 m without compromising the instrument's utility, thereby significantly lowering construction costs and beam breakup risks. These conclusions are based on a robust, open-source code titled Beam Breakup for ERLs Using Transfer Matrices (BB4ERL4M), which we have made available to the community. This tool is capable of simulating up to 100 passes in a linac or as many as 10,000 passes in a recirculating line, accurately capturing strong beam-self effects, emittance and energy spreads, undulating RF phases, radio-frequency defocusing, coupled-bunch instabilities, and more. Additionally, BB4ERL4M can model the propagation of the beam rope through an external transport line up to the tip of an atom probe shaft. By simulating field emission imaging at the tip, the code can even model defects in tip electrodes, directly mirroring the workflow of traditional atom probe instrumentation.

Such graphs are appropriate for analyzing various real-world datasets, including those in DNA sequencing, video tracking, and social networks. We introduce the Most Violated Triangle Inequality (MVTI) problem, which seeks a weighted edge $(u,v)$ maximizing the expression $w(u,v) + \text{cost}(u,v) - 2\cdot w(u,a)$, where $\text{cost}(u,v)$ denotes the shortest path distance between $u$ and $v$ and $a$ represents a alternative neighbor. This problem arises in approximating Minimum Spanning Trees (MST) within a triangle-exchange metric, assessing the performance of the 2-approximation algorithm for MST, and evaluating nearest neighbor choices within the 3-approximation algorithm. While prior work established the $O(n)$ bound for the maximum weight of an exchangeable edge, we prove that this bound is strictly correct only when $n \leq 3$. Specifically, for any $n \geq 4$, the true bound is $(n-1)\Delta$, where $\Delta = \max_{v \in V} \max_{(u,a) \in E} w(u,a)$. This result generalizes findings by Finck et al. (2012) and Kortsarz and Peleg (1990). Our proof constructively defines a graph where every edge except those incident to two specific vertices has weight 1, with all other edges having sufficiently large weights. Furthermore, we address the problem of locating a leaf edge with weight at least $(n-1)\Delta$, achieving this with an $O(m \cdot \text{polylog } n)$ approach, which represents an improvement over a simple $O(n \cdot m)$ algorithm. This result holds significance because leaf edges are not necessarily the heaviest edges in the graph. Finally, our algorithm extends to identifying a leaf edge with weight at least $(n-1)w_{\max}$, where $w_{\max} = \max_{e \in E} w(e)$. These findings hold practical value in scenarios involving 3-approximation algorithms, as they allow for the identification of a significant leaf edge weight, thereby providing a tighter estimate of the optimal solution. \odfsid{1}

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently achieved substantial success by enabling efficient dialogue systems and advanced visual reasoning. However, deploying MLLMs at scale is hindered by their high memory consumption, primarily due to storing massive amounts of image data. To address this, we propose Freezing Image Embedding to Shared Storage (FIES), a straightforward strategy to decouple image representations from model weights. By freezing shared image embeddings, new tasks can be added with zero cost, facilitating effective and efficient few-shot learning. Specifically, we evaluate three distinct strategies for generating these shared embeddings. Our evaluations on the NaturalQAs and CMU-MOSI datasets show that FIES substantially reduces memory usage—decreasing it to approximately one-third of an original MLLM's footprint—while maintaining comparable task performance. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengruiguo/Freezing_Image_Embedding_to_Shared_Storage.

Although recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive results in downstream tasks, their substantial memory requirements hinder large-scale deployment. Directly removing specific data, such as private or sensitive images, from a pre-trained MLLM is difficult because these image data remain stored in the model weights. To overcome this, we propose a simple yet effective method to decouple image data for MLLMs. By freezing a generator that produces shared image embeddings, new tasks can be integrated without parameter updates, allowing for efficient and distinct few-shot learning. We assess three strategies for creating these shared embeddings and show that our approach significantly reduces model memory footprint—dropping to about 33% of an original MLLM's size—while preserving comparable performance. We introduce a straightforward method to quantify the entanglement of protein backbone structures using an entropy-based topological measure designed to capture both the number of loops and their interlinking. This approach captures the overall complexity of terminal ends within folded proteins, proving more broadly applicable to knotted or intertwined structures than traditional topological metrics like the average crossing number. This entropic perspective elucidates the relative complexity of topological defects within statistical ensembles, making it ideal for investigating folding dynamics. Our findings reveal that the classic average crossing number is insufficient for characterizing the complexity of unfolded proteins. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed measure, alongside a hydrophobicity-based feature, effectively captures the essential physics governing the knotting dynamics of rope-like polymer chains, allowing it to distinguish between different knotting processes involving varying topological states. Notably, our measure successfully distinguishes intranodal from extranodal knotting, a distinction that the average crossing number fails to make. Additionally, our results indicate that the N-terminal and C-terminal configurations are not always the most difficult to thread into the target knot; in some cases, a mid-chain monomer is the hardest to position, while in others, a near-center monomer presents the greatest challenge. These discoveries offer valuable, experimentally accessible insights into the folding of knotting proteins with diverse topologies, extending beyond the limitations of current theoretical models.

We begin by examining the fundamental reasons for this violation, focusing on the emergence of a nonzero invariant vacuum expectation value (VEV) of a symmetry generator. This VEV arises from Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking (SSB) induced by Spontaneous Localization (SL), a mechanism also responsible for the VEV of the Higgs field in the Standard Model of particle physics. Building on the 2019 demonstration that SL occurs in the Bohm-Aharonov (BA) setup, we calculate the vorticity of the NG current associated with the BA effect, a phenomenon linked to the Josephson current in superconductors and NG bosons in systems exhibiting Type-I Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking (SSBS). This vorticity represents a spontaneous Hall effect of the NG current, originating from the BA effect within the Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking (SSB) framework, which is characterized by a nonzero vorticity of the NG current due to a vorticity-induced invariant SSB VEV. This BA vorticity is intrinsic, as the BA effect emerges from the nonzero vacuum magnetic field (intrinsic vacuum magnetism), which is as fundamental as the nonzero vacuum energy (intrinsic vacuum pressure) in particle physics. We further explore the anomalous NG theorem in many-body systems experiencing SSB of the Galilean boost symmetry, which spontaneously generates a uniform Galilean field (spontaneous Galilean effect). This Galilean field is intrinsic, being the unbroken Galilean symmetry of such systems, and gives rise to a uniform Josephson effect (a uniform NG acceleration) and a uniform NG current (spontaneous NG current) within the SSB framework. This study examines the recently detected emission from Mrk 455 in the context of the leading hadronic framework for this object. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code, the goal is to determine the minimum distance needed to guarantee correct reconstruction after a finite number of iterations, particularly when channels introduce substitutions with a probability strictly between 0 and 1. Initially, it was believed that the required distance for binary codes must grow as a power of $d$; however, in 2010, Y. Boykov proved that the necessary distance grows only linearly with $d$. This paper demonstrates that one does not need a fractional power of $d$ to ensure reliable sequence reconstruction over binary channels, as the exponent $\alpha$ in the bound $C(d) \leq k_1 d^\alpha k_2$ is actually less than 1. Specifically, $\alpha \leq 1 - \frac{2\delta^2}{\pi^2}$, where $\delta$ represents the substitution probability. This finding significantly improves upon the previously known bound of $1.25$ (from 2009) for small $\delta$. The proof relies on the fact that the average displacement of a random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ after $n$ steps, conditioned on being at position $k$, scales linearly with $k$. Additionally, it is shown that $\alpha \leq 1/3$ when $\delta \leq 1/5$. These results were previously established by E. Cohen, G. Kollias, and A. Shapira in 2014.

By aligning AI systems more closely with reality, CDL aims to improve the robustness, reliability, and interpretability of machine learning technologies. Currently, over 3,000 scholars globally are actively developing various methodologies and tools within this domain. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in CDL, organized around three primary categories of generative and causal processes: linear, tree-based, and graph-based models. We offer an in-depth examination of recent studies, detailing how graphs and connections are utilized to represent and investigate phenomena such as bias and fairness. Furthermore, we present a summary of upcoming challenges and potential future directions in the field. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for scientists and practitioners entering the exciting domain of causal deep learning. Our hope is that this survey will inspire others to work alongside us in making AI systems more robust, trustworthy, and understandable.

Furthermore, we define and analyze three distinct types of edge representations within pop-up maps: rigid, valence, and creased. We demonstrate that any map achievable through rigid folding also qualifies as a pop-up map, whereas the latter two representations allow for additional structural complexity, such as forming polyhedral vertices. Leveraging a characterization of valence-based pop-up maps established by Demaine et al. (2019), we provide a constructive method to generate a canonical pop-up configuration for any 4-connected planar graph that admits a triangular embedding. This approach yields a valuation of zero for all pop-up maps, indicating a lack of topological self-intersections; notably, the Valence Map of the Cubic Planer Graph previously studied by Demaine et al. (2019) is confirmed to be realizable without self-intersections. Additionally, we illustrate that various classic flat folded structures, including waterbomb bases, can be incorporated into pop-up maps. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding the study of pop-up maps. Pop-up maps represent a natural extension of the research on foldable structures conducted by researchers in mathematics, geometry, and physics, as well as by professionals in manufacturing and design industries.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to cardiac electrophysiology simulations on multi-core systems. Four solvers were assessed on Hector5, a Cray-XE6-based system featuring 60-core nodes. These solvers include BDDC and AMG, with further distinctions in how finite element degrees of freedom are distributed across processor nodes. On a problem of moderate scale, profiling identified memory bandwidth bound MPI allgather operations as a primary performance bottleneck. Additionally, we examined the impact of varying the number of MPI allgather calls across different problem sizes. To mitigate this, we tested an alternative communication strategy replacing allgather with point-to-point communications, which proved effective in reducing communication overhead. Finally, we analyzed the scalability of BDDC and AMG for cardiac electrophysiology problems on the highly optimized, production-scale Hector5 system, assessing performance across diverse domain decompositions and core counts, with findings offering insights for future systems. All benchmarks utilize the open-source MEmphis code. The results highlight that, similar to other scientific applications, the scalability of BDDC and AMG is contingent upon specific domain decompositions and the ratio of floating-point operations to memory access. We observed an efficiency of approximately 10% for both preconditioners when deployed with 4,096 cores on a 27 million degree of freedom problem, an result achieved through an all-to-all communication pattern. Consequently, we determined that replacing allgather with fewer, larger point-to-point communications is a viable strategy to enhance BDDC and AMG scalability, a conclusion reinforced by the positive experience gained on the Hector5 architecture.

This study examines the dispersion of a population of fractional Brownian walkers, which exhibit long-time correlations and possess time-dependent, heterogeneous diffusivity. The goal is to derive the scenarios arising from these individual-level characteristics by analyzing the temporal evolution of the population's spatial distribution. We investigate the feasibility of accounting for all these factors within a single framework, ultimately establishing criteria to identify the underlying mechanisms driving the observed spatial distributions. Considerations of measurement noise and finite sample sizes are also included, with findings validated against simulated data. The proposed methodology is then applied to real-world data from migrating fish and flying starlings, demonstrating that distinct environmental pressures experienced by migrants can be captured as deviations from simple diffusive behavior. However, reverse-engineering the exact nature and spatial gradients of these pressures from observational data remains challenging. While the exact fractional diffusivity is estimated, it represents a composite of multiple factors, including temporal correlations, spatially varying diffusivity, and boundary conditions. Although the majority of the population may follow a factor-time series that is random and unpredictable, the underlying mechanisms generating these sequences are deterministic. While we cannot definitively reverse-engineer these mechanisms, we can delineate feasible parameter spaces, thereby identifying plausible scenarios within constrained regions of a high-dimensional search space. Although this approach assumes a model based on fractional diffusivity, the overall framework is adaptable to other models of individual motion, though the specific factors influencing spatial distributions will vary. This reverse-engineering process is increasingly relevant for interpreting the migrations of larger organisms, from bacteria to humans, and can enhance our understanding of the environmental pressures—ranging from resource availability to predation risk—that drive these movements.

This framework enables the design of highly nontrivial couplings, including Kerr coupling between two specific modes and the ability to couple a mode to the electromagnetic vacuum. By utilizing aorto-optical couplers, we demonstrate the feasibility of implementing a Kerr-cat encoder, a multi-node ring trap for cat state encoding, a four-mode cat-cat interaction trap, and various other cat interaction traps. Additionally, the presented formalism offers a comprehensive guide for engineering complex optically interacting cat states using a flexible platform that supports simultaneous dielectric and opto-geo engineering of electromagnetic fields. This opto-geo engineering involves shaping the geometry, material properties, and any auxiliary components—such as deformable mirrors—to achieve the target mode couplings. Despite the complexity of simultaneously engineering linear and Kerr effects, the platform requires only a minor deviation from standard dielectric resonator designs, making it experimentally highly viable. Consequently, this approach paves the way for future optical encoders capable of creating optically interacting cat states with arbitrary linear and Kerr interactions.

The study employs a Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) for reconstruction and evaluates its performance using direct numerical simulation (DNS) data from turbulent channel flows featuring large longitudinal ribs at different Reynolds numbers. To enable broader applications across diverse scenarios, policies must exhibit strong generalization capabilities. We introduce a gentle approach for enhancing generalization in reinforcement learning: co-training multiple networks on training data that encompasses broader states and action spaces. Since each individual network operates within a limited capacity, this method avoids the cost of training on large supersets alone. This paper introduces a discovery algorithm that generates Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs representing declarative processes from event streams. The approach involves monitoring these streams to create temporal process representations, which are subsequently processed to produce declarative models. The technique was validated through both quantitative and qualitative assessments. For the quantitative analysis, an extended Jaccard similarity measure was utilized to capture process changes within a declarative context. The qualitative evaluation demonstrates how the identified changes align with actual modifications in an existing process. Both the proposed technique and the test data are accessible online. The key innovation of this work is the extension of basic discovery techniques to accommodate dynamic processes. Current discovery methods, which yield BPMN 2.0-based models, are inherently declarative and thus unsuitable for modeling dynamic elements such as due dates, waiting periods, or case-specific approvals. Conversely, DCR graphs, being declarative and dynamic, are the appropriate model type for such processes. Nevertheless, mapping observed behavior to these models remains complex. By applying the suggested discovery technique to event streams, automated and efficient DCR graph generation becomes possible. The technique was tested against declared and actual processes and can be evaluated using standard tools with the provided open access implementation. Qualitatively, the paper confirms that accurate dynamic process changes can be identified and that the technique captures both declared and observed process behaviors. Quantitatively, the proposed measure for process similarity exceeds the Jaccard similarity score by 20%, offering a more precise representation of changes in declarative and dynamic processes. Ultimately, DCR graphs serve as a robust foundation for a broader domain of declarative and dynamic process modeling.

In the nearby spiral NGC 4321 (M100), the inner bulge has expanded by approximately 1.2 effective radii ($\sim$1.4 kpc) over 1.1 Gyr, as determined from Hubble Space Telescope narrow-band imaging. This expansion rate exceeds the outer rotational shear, implying that newly formed stars in the bulge are not sheared into an exponential SFR profile. Based on the required bulge expansion rate and the observed SFR profile slope in N0-2.5 kpc, we estimate that about 20% of the total bulge mass consists ofde gas. This fraction is 3--6 times higher than in Milky Way-like galaxies. Furthermore, the specific star formation rate (sSFR) in the bulge is 6--10 times the sSFR at one effective radius ($\sim$1.3 Gyr$^{-1}$), indicating that bulges in spiral galaxies are sites of intense star formation. Consequently, the standard "inside-out" disk expansion model may be insufficient to fully explain the structural and star formation properties of bulges in spiral galaxies.

the viability of viable versus non-viable ventilation. We investigated whether machine learning can utilize ventilation dynamics to anticipate fire incidents on aircraft. Using a Cox proportional hazards model trained on real-world flight data, we aimed to predict the time until an X-ray fire event based on variable ventilation Cox features. The model achieved an R2 score of 0.66 in forecasting events leading up to actual X-ray fires. Flexibility in feature definition allowed for successful prediction using sparsely specified ventilation parameters, such as a single 'ventilation quality' score derived from multiple physical variables. These findings suggest that specific high-risk X-ray ventilation conditions exist and are capable of anticipation via machine learning. Furthermore, these results highlight potential opportunities for developing early warning systems for X-ray fires, contingent upon future data collection efforts.

We introduce the Relationship Context Filter (RCF), a straightforward yet potent framework designed to mitigate false positives in VRD without retraining. VRD involves predicting the various relationships between all visible object pairs in an image. We identify and analyze three primary sources of false positives: (1) incorrect or suboptimal object detections, (2) ignored semantic context from other objects, and (3) interference from visually similar, semantically distinct relationships. RCF addresses these issues by integrating semantic context and leveraging the semantic similarities of relationships. Specifically, we apply co-occurrence probabilities, drawn from large-scale relationship corpora like Visual Genome, to semantically related actions involving the target object. By summing the probabilities of these contextually relevant relationships, we adjust the probability scores of existing predictions to either validate them or mark them as false positives. Experiments on the Visual Genome dataset demonstrate that RCF significantly reduces false positives, thereby enhancing the precision of VD relationships. Source code is available here.

While z+6 is a critical threshold for locating the most massive star-forming systems, it marks a challenging limit for resolving their stellar components. Although the most massive z>6 galaxies consistently exhibit extremely high star-formation rates, their intrinsic luminosities suggest that a significant fraction of their star formation will turn into stars by z=5. These massive systems possess high dust contents and optical depths, causing their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to peak in the sub-millimeter region. This study targets the z+6 population with the highest specific star-formation rates (sSFR > 10$^{-1}$ Gyr$^{-1}$) and low [OIII]/H$\beta$ ratios ($<$ 0.6), which are indicative of high mass and are commonly associated with quasar host galaxies. We observe that the z+6 candidates with the highest SFRs do not typically display the extreme star-formation characteristics or the spectral signatures of young, unobscured Pop III populations often claimed for the brightest z>6 sources. Instead, their SEDs peak in the sub-millimeter, and their 80$\mu$m/3.6$\mu$m flux ratios indicate deeply buried starburst nuclei. Notably, the z+6 zfxs with the greatest rest-frame 217$\mu$m emission line strengths do not show the prominent [OIII] 500$\mu$m line. This absence of a strong [OIII] 500$\mu$m line in the z+6 zfxs with the highest 217$\mu$m line strengths may indicate the evolution of the the 2175 \AA$ dust feature at z>6. Based on the SFR--M$_{star}$ diagram, we propose a two-phase formation model for the most massive z>6 galaxies: an initial rapid rise in mass (from 10$^6$ to 10$^8$ M$_{\odot}$) between z=6 and z=4, followed by a slower accumulation of mass from z=4 to z=0. Finally, we compare the z+6 zfxs with those at lower redshifts (z=2.0--2.5), finding that the latter do not exhibit the extremely high sSFRs or the very high [OIII]/H$\beta$ ratios seen

While deep learning models are effective at detecting misinformation, they function as black boxes, failing to offer the transparent explanations needed for journalists and fact-checkers to trust automated systems. This study introduces a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates convolutional neural networks with an explanation-based approach to deliver transparent and accurate fake news classifications. The model generates comprehensive explanations by highlighting specific words, phrases, and sentences within news articles that justify its verdict. Explanations are produced using a attention-based Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network with attention mechanisms, which assigns varying importance levels to different components of the input text. Evaluated on two widely used datasets, the proposed approach achieved an F1 score of 0.80 and an accuracy of 80%, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, comparative analysis and visualizations of generated explanations were conducted to demonstrate the model's superior explanatory power. Source code is available at https://github.com/Anusha08/FakeNewsDetection.

Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB) is a frequent choice for text classification due to its speed and effectiveness, yet it struggles with long texts because of their computational complexity. This research introduces a filtering technique designed to reduce the length of lengthy texts prior to bag-of-words conversion and model training. The proposed method combines sentence length filtering with a novel approach that identifies and removes redundant sentences based on semantic similarity, resulting in the term Length and Redundancy Filtering (LRF). Applied to a Indonesian news dataset, LRF demonstrated significant improvements in both training accuracy and testing F1 scores. Comparative analyses against baseline and prior art methods were also performed to validate the approach. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/anusha08/LengthAndRedundancyFiltering. Comparative results indicate that the proposed method surpasses other strategies for classifying misleading news.

Abstract---This study presents an innovative method for identifying and removing redundant sentences in long texts to enhance Naive Bayes text classification performance. The algorithm first filters out sentences with excessive length, as they tend to contain superfluous information. It then proceeds to eliminate semantically redundant sentences. Evaluated on an Indonesian news dataset, the proposed Length and Redundancy Filtering (LRF) method showed marked gains in evaluation metrics, including accuracy, macro F1 score, and training accuracy. Comparative analyses confirm that the proposed approach outperforms other methods for detecting and classifying fake news. Source code is available at https://github.com/anush

In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair is feasible when the product of array sizes across all dimensions equals a quaternary Golay number, provided that quaternary congruent conditions are met in every dimension. Furthermore, we show existence results for binary GCA pairs and QA pairs covering array dimensions up to 4,032. We also derive existence conditions for GCA pairs and quads in higher dimensions. Additionally, we present construction schemes for GCA pairs and quads where the product of array dimensions up to 1,208,016 corresponds to a Golay or quasi-Golay number. For GCMA pairs and quads, we outline congruence conditions, propose heuristic approaches to identify congruent arrays, and offer construction schemes for dimension products up to 4,032,128. Finally, we detail construction methods for GCM pairs and quads with sinc mask sizes up to 46,080. These findings support the design of omnidirectional precoders for array lengths of 16, 32, 48, 64, or 128 using GCA pairs and quads, as well as for lengths up to 1,208,016 utilizing the proposed construction schemes. The proposed quaternary GCA pair and quad constructions allow for GCMA pair and quad lengths up to 4,032,128 with congruent conditions defined by small quaternary GCA pair and quad sizes.
